newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian rupee kept down by central bank action.
newsitem.headline: Indian rupee kept down by central bank action.

text.p: Sustained dollar purchases by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) since January has prevented the Indian rupee from appreciating against the dollar in the past two months, dealers said on Thursday.
They said the dollar supply in the market far exceeded demand and the rupee could have moved up to 35.65 per dollar had the central bank not intervened.
The Indian unit was trading at 35.862/872 at noon on Thursday.
Even the redemption of foreign currency bonds worth around $1.1 billion in January and February did not have much impact on the rupee-dollar exchange rate, dealers added.

"RBI has been buying dollars right from January," said a dealer at a foreign bank. "It's not as if they came into the market only this week. Had they not been buying dollars, we could have seen the rupee at 35.65 or even higher."
While precise figures were not available, it was likely that the bank had bought around US$50 million a day through mid-January and February, he said.
"This week, RBI has probably bought around $300 million so far," the dealer said.
Aggressive buying from the central bank was necessary to prevent a sharp rise earlier this week.

On Monday, the Indian rupee closed at 35.825/835 per dollar against last Friday's close of 35.89/90 despite dollar purchases by the RBI. The central bank bought dollars again on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Dealers said the central bank intervention was required to prevent a rise in the rupee that would affect India's exports, making them more expensive.
The dollar supply has been good and in the absence of import demand, and the rupee has shown a tendency to strengthen.
Dealers said the sources of the dollar supply were varied, ranging from foreign direct and portfolio investments to proceeds from exports and foreign borrowing.
"At the moment, foreign portfolio investments are not really big," said a dealer. "But they should start coming in soon."
A rise in the value of the dollar against other foreign currencies has not had much impact on the rupee-dollar exchange rate, but dealers said inflation needed to be factored in.

"That (inflation) is the key thing," said one dealer. "The rupee will have to depreciate if the exchange rate is to be realistic and take into account inflation differentials between India and the U.S."
Indian year-on-year inflation, as measured by the wholesale price index, was 7.99 percent in February. U.S. inflation as measured by the producer price index was 2.5 percent in January.
